title: Broth, Stock, and Consommé: What Is the Difference?

seo.title: Broth vs Stock vs Consommé: Differences
seo.meta_description: Stock is usually an unsalted or lightly seasoned cooking base with body from bones and connective tissue; broth is more ready-to-eat and seasoned; consommé is a clarified, concentrated soup. Packaged labels can blur the boundaries.
seo.search_intent: Explain the culinary differences among broth, stock, and consommé and how packaged products may overlap.

excerpt: Stock is usually built as a cooking foundation and often gets body from bones; broth is generally more seasoned and ready to eat; consommé is a clarified, concentrated soup. These are useful culinary distinctions, not perfectly standardized supermarket categories.
content_html:
Three clear liquids can sit beside each other in the grocery aisle and all look like “broth,” yet a cook may use the words stock, broth, and consommé for different jobs. The distinctions are clearest in technique: stock is a foundation, broth is closer to a finished seasoned liquid, and consommé is clarified and concentrated.

Stock is built for body and later cooking

Traditional stock commonly uses bones, connective tissue, vegetables and aromatics. It is often left unsalted or only lightly seasoned so it can reduce in sauces and soups without becoming too salty. Gelatin gives well-made stock body.

Broth is generally more ready to serve

Broth often includes more meat, seasoning and salt and is intended to taste complete enough to drink or serve as a simple soup. In home cooking the boundaries overlap: a chicken broth can certainly contain bones, and a stock can contain meat.

Consommé adds clarification

Classic consommé starts with a flavorful stock or broth and is clarified, traditionally with a protein-rich raft that traps suspended particles. The result is clear but intensely flavored rather than merely a thin broth.

Supermarket names are less strict than kitchen definitions

Commercial broth and stock can have similar ingredients and nutrition. Compare sodium, protein and ingredients if those details matter to the recipe. Use the culinary names to predict function, then use the package to see what the product actually contains.

faq.question: Is stock always made from bones?
faq.answer: Traditional stock often relies heavily on bones and connective tissue, but real recipes and commercial products can overlap with broth.

faq.question: Is broth more seasoned than stock?
faq.answer: Usually. Broth is often intended to be palatable on its own, while stock is commonly a lightly seasoned cooking base.

faq.question: What makes consommé different?
faq.answer: It is a clarified, concentrated soup made from a flavorful stock or broth, giving a clear appearance and intense flavor.
